text:
We finally moved our billing service off the 2017-era Postgres 9.6 cluster last weekend — 14 months after we first scoped it. Some things I didn't expect:

— The logical replication lag was fine; the sequences were not. We forgot to sync them and the first 40 minutes of new invoices collided with old IDs.
— Our ORM silently relied on an implicit cast that PG 15 no longer allows. Three endpoints returned 500s until Priya found it.
— The rollback plan was never used — but writing it forced us to find two cron jobs nobody owned.

Total downtime: 11 minutes, mostly DNS TTL. If you're planning a similar jump, sync your sequences before cutover — I'll die on that hill.
label: human

text:
After nine years at Kestrel Logistics I handed back my badge on Friday. I want to write this down while it's still fresh — partly for me, partly because a few people have asked what actually happened.

I joined in 2017 as the second data analyst. We were tracking driver hours in a shared Excel file that crashed every Monday. By 2021 we had a proper warehouse in BigQuery, a dispatch-forecasting model that cut empty miles by about 11% on the Midlands routes, and a team of six. I'm proud of that — genuinely.

The last eighteen months were harder. After the acquisition, our roadmap was rewritten three times, and two of the people I hired were let go in the March round. I stayed longer than I should have — mostly out of loyalty to the people still there, a little bit out of fear.

What I'm doing next: I start at a small cold-chain startup in Leeds on 4 November — pharmaceutical deliveries, temperature telemetry, about 40 people. It's a step down in title and a step up in how much I'll get to build. I'm nervous about going from a team of six back to a team of one — I haven't written production Python daily since 2020.

Things I'd tell my 2017 self:
— Write down why a model exists, not just how it works. Nobody remembered why the Tuesday adjustment was there.
— Get to know the drivers. The best feature in our forecast came from a conversation with Dave in the Coventry depot about school-run traffic.
— Leave before you're bitter, not after.

Thank you to Ana, Tomasz, Ruth and Kwame. You know what you did.

Two years ago I couldn't run 5k without stopping. Yesterday: Berlin Marathon, 3:28:41 — 9 minutes off my Valencia time.

Splits:
5k 24:31
10k 49:02
Half 1:43:50
30k 2:28:10
35k 2:52:44
40k 3:17:55

The plan was 4:55/km flat. I held it until 32k, then the Tiergarten stretch hurt more than I expected and I dropped to 5:10s. Took 6 gels (Maurten 100, every 35 min) and had no stomach issues this time, which was the main thing I changed after Valencia.

Biggest lesson: the 18-week block with two midweek medium-long runs worked better for me than the higher-mileage plan I tried last year. I was less tired going in.

Thank you to Jule for standing at km 38 with a sign that just said 'WHY'. Fair question.

text:
Making my grandma's pierogi for the church sale Saturday, sharing the dough recipe since a few of you asked:

3 cups flour
1 egg
1/2 cup sour cream
1/2 cup warm water
1 tbsp melted butter
pinch of salt

Mix, knead 5 minutes, rest covered 30 min. Roll thin (about 1/8 in). Filling is potato + farmer's cheese + lots of fried onion. Boil until they float plus 2 minutes, then pan-fry in butter. Freeze them on a sheet pan BEFORE boiling if you're making ahead or they stick together. We did 240 last year and sold out by noon 😊

text:
What we learned shipping offline mode in our field-inspection app (6 months, 3 engineers):

1. Conflict resolution is the whole project. We went with last-write-wins per field, not per record. Per-record LWW lost inspector notes in 7% of beta syncs.
2. SQLite on Android is fine; IndexedDB on iOS Safari is not. We hit storage eviction on older iPads within two weeks.
3. Show sync state honestly. Our 'Saved' badge used to mean saved locally. Inspectors assumed it meant uploaded. We now show 'On device' vs 'Synced'.
4. Test airplane mode in an actual basement. Our office Wi-Fi never dropped the way a parking garage does.

Happy to share our merge function if anyone is working on the same problem.
label: human

In an era defined by relentless disruption, the organizations that thrive are not necessarily the biggest or the fastest — they are the most adaptable.

As we navigate an increasingly complex landscape shaped by artificial intelligence, shifting workforce expectations, and evolving customer needs, one truth stands out: transformation is no longer optional. It is a strategic imperative.

But what does true transformation look like?

🔹 It starts with mindset. Leaders must foster a culture of curiosity, where experimentation is encouraged and failure is reframed as a stepping stone to innovation.

🔹 It requires alignment. Technology investments only unlock their full potential when they are tightly aligned with business objectives and human-centered design.

🔹 It demands empathy. In a world of constant change, people need psychological safety to bring their authentic selves to work.

🔹 It thrives on collaboration. Breaking down silos enables cross-functional teams to co-create solutions that deliver meaningful, measurable value.

Ultimately, the future belongs to those who are willing to embrace uncertainty, invest in their people, and lead with purpose. The journey is not always linear, but it is always worth it.

At the intersection of technology and humanity lies an incredible opportunity — to build organizations that are not only more efficient, but more resilient, inclusive, and future-ready.

The question is not whether change will come. The question is whether we will be ready to lead it.

What steps is your organization taking to future-proof its workforce? I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments. 👇

My 7-year-old just taught me the most important lesson about sales.

We were at the park yesterday.

She walked up to a group of kids she'd never met.

No pitch deck.
No cold email sequence.
No LinkedIn automation.

She just said: 'Can I play?'

And they said yes.

That's when it hit me.

We overcomplicate everything in B2B.

We hide behind templates, funnels, and frameworks.

But at the end of the day, people buy from people.

Here's what my daughter knows that most sales reps don't:

1️⃣ Curiosity beats scripts
2️⃣ Authenticity beats polish
3️⃣ Asking beats assuming
4️⃣ Showing up beats overthinking

Kids don't fear rejection. Somewhere along the way, we learn to.

Maybe it's time we unlearned it.
